issues.legal_issue: A revenue record identifying a person as an occupant does not, without more, establish that the person acquired title to the property.
material_facts: The property had substantial value, and no registered instrument transferring it to the claimant had been executed.
The revenue entry described the claimant and the prior holder as occupants; the claimant relied on it as proof of title.
issues.conclusion: The entry could support a presumption of the claimant’s possession, but not of her title.
issues.legal_principle: A revenue entry may support a presumption concerning possession, but in the circumstances here it did not establish title. The Court distinguished the reliance on revenue entries in Gangabai v. Fakirgowda Somaypagowda Desai and Desai Navinkant Kesarlal v. Prabhat Kabhai.

predicates.revenue_entry_offered_to_prove_title: A party relied on a revenue record as evidence that the party acquired title to property.
predicates.entry_identified_person_as_occupant: The revenue record described the person relying on it as an occupant rather than recording a transfer of title.
predicates.no_registered_transfer_was_executed: No registered instrument transferring the property to that person was executed.

issues.definition: When a party relies on an occupant entry without an executed registered transfer, the entry supports possession rather than title.

issues.legal_issue: Account-book entries should be rejected as unreliable when no witness supports their correctness and relevant corroborating material is withheld.
material_facts: The account books were admitted subject to objections, and the person who had written some entries said he had done so on another family member’s instructions and could not vouch for their reliability.
The person who produced and controlled the books did not testify or call a witness to support their correctness.
Other documents that could have supported the books and the asserted joint-family account were not produced.
issues.conclusion: The account books were not reliable and were rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 makes qualifying entries in regularly kept books of account relevant, but the Court did not accept the entries as reliable on this record because their correctness was unsupported and material corroborating documents were withheld.

rule.if: civil_property_dispute and account_books_relied_on and nobody_supported_entry_correctness and important_corroborating_records_withheld

predicates.civil_property_dispute: The court was deciding a civil dispute concerning rights in property.
predicates.account_books_relied_on: A party relied on entries in account books to support its account of the parties’ property dealings.
predicates.nobody_supported_entry_correctness: No witness accepted responsibility for the correctness of the relevant entries.
predicates.important_corroborating_records_withheld: A party with access to relevant supporting records did not produce them.

issues.definition: In a civil property dispute, relied-on account books are rejected as unreliable when no witness supports their correctness and important corroborating records are withheld.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant may establish adverse possession of a landlord’s interest through tenants without personally occupying the property when the tenants attorn to the claimant and the claimant’s hostile possession is demonstrated in a manner suited to the property.
material_facts: Most of the rooms in the property were occupied by tenants, who paid rent to the claimant under receipts identifying the property as hers.

During part of the relevant period, the claimant received the rents through an agent; after a dispute, she took direct charge of management, and possession through her family continued until the suit was filed.
The claimant’s evidence established hostile and exclusive control for more than the required limitation period.
issues.conclusion: The tenants’ physical occupation did not prevent the claimant from acquiring title by adverse possession; her possession as landlord through them was sufficient in the circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and the corresponding reference to an interest in immovable property in Article 144 of the Limitation Act, 1908, adverse possession depends on an intention to claim exclusive title demonstrated through possession appropriate to the nature of the property. A landlord’s possession may be exercised through tenants who attorn to the claimant and pay rent to that claimant. The Court relied on Uppalapati Veera Venkata Satyanarayanaraju v. Josyula Hanumayamma and distinguished the argument based on Hari Prasad Agarwalla v. Abdul Haq.

rule.if: adverse_possession_claim and property_held_by_tenants and tenants_attorned_to_claimant and rent_paid_to_claimant_under_ownership_assertions and claimant_exercised_hostile_exclusive_landlord_control and possession_met_limitation_period

predicates.adverse_possession_claim: A party claimed title to property through adverse possession.
predicates.property_held_by_tenants: Tenants, rather than the competing claimants, physically occupied the property.
predicates.tenants_attorned_to_claimant: The tenants recognized the claimant as the person entitled to receive rent.
predicates.rent_paid_to_claimant_under_ownership_as: The tenants paid rent to the claimant under receipts that asserted the claimant’s ownership.
predicates.claimant_exercised_hostile_exclusive_lan: The claimant exercised control over the landlord’s interest in a manner hostile and exclusive to the competing owner.
predicates.possession_met_limitation_period: The claimant’s hostile possession, including possession exercised through tenants or representatives, continued for the period required to acquire title.

issues.definition: When tenants occupy property but recognize the claimant as landlord, pay rent under ownership assertions, and the claimant exercises hostile and exclusive landlord control for the required period, the claimant acquires title by adverse possession.

issues.legal_issue: An agent who collects rent for a principal cannot treat that agency possession as the agent’s own joint possession against the principal.
material_facts: A family member managed the property and collected rent from tenants on the claimant’s behalf during part of the period in dispute.
The claimant relied on the rent collection as conduct by her agent, while the opposing side argued that the collector’s activity showed joint possession.
issues.conclusion: The rent collector’s possession was attributable to the claimant as principal, and the collector could not claim his own joint possession on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 182 and 188 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the agent acts for the principal within the scope of the agency; possession by an agent is the principal’s possession, and the fiduciary relationship prevents the agent from asserting that possession as his own against the principal. The Court relied on David Lyell v. John Lawson Kennedy, Williams v. Pott, and Secretary of State for India v. Krishnamoni Gupta.

predicates.possession_dispute_in_principal_agent_re: A dispute arose over whether conduct by an agent amounted to possession against the principal.
predicates.agent_collected_rent_for_principal: A person collected rent from tenants on behalf of a principal under an agency relationship.
predicates.agent_claimed_own_joint_possession_from_: The agent relied on collecting rent for the principal as a basis to claim personal or joint possession against the principal.

issues.definition: When a rent-collecting agent relies on that agency activity to claim personal or joint possession against the principal, the agent cannot claim independent joint possession.
